newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FOCUS-Argentina has come far but still more to do.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Argentina has come far but still more to do.

text.p: Argentina's economy has improved sharply in recent years but the country still has far to go before it attracts sufficient confidence to get a sovereign investment-grade credit rating, bankers and officials said at a conference this week.
"If we are objective Argentina still has some way to go before it is investment grade," said Arturo Porzecanski, head of fixed income research and chief economist for the Americas at ING Barings.
Standard & Poor's rates Argentina BB, two notches below investment-grade and Moody's has it at B1.

Gerald Corrigan, managing director of Goldman Sachs & Co. and former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, said Argentina's economic reforms in recent years have been "nothing short of astonishing."

But he also warned Argentina's commitment to policy discipline needs to be maintained "because a failure to maintain that discipline will surely give rise to a repeat of the painful experience of the 1980s."
That bittersweet sensation of Argentina's economy was borne out by other speakers during the three-day annual conference of the Argentine Banking Association ending Wednesday.
Wendell Stark, the chief investment officer at Invesco Capital Management reminded the audience that "there is a feeling that there are still problems," that need to be resolved.
Among them are investor concerns that efforts on the fiscal front could ease in the face of approaching mid-term elections and near record high unemployment at 17.3 percent.

Argentina may already have met many of the economic targets achieved by BBB investment-grade rated countries, as Undersecretary of Finance Miguel Kiguel argued should merit an investment-grade ranking.
But as U.S. economist Rudiger Dornbusch pointed out: "It takes time. It is a long-distance race and you do not just buy a pair of shoes and say "now I am Maradona"."
"Argentina has made fantastic progress and I have every confidence that over the next five years Argentina will look increasingly like Chile," he added.

That time element is crucial though, speakers said. Chile started reforming 15 years ago and Argentina's process only kicked off around 1990, after a decade during which one speaker said most economists genuinely viewed the country as a lost "basket case."

Compared with Chile, "countries that did not service their debt in the 1980s are punished," the Economy Ministry's chief advisor Carlos Rodriguez said. "What do we have to do to improve this? We have to make them forget."
While Argentina's annual inflation is one of the lowest in the world at 0.1 percent and growth looks set to rise to six percent this year, there are other important barriers holding the country back.

The president of the Argentine Central Bank, Pedro Pou, discussed one of those obstacles in his speech. "Having achieved the objective of price stability, we should focus our work on the efficiency of the banking industry, with the objective of achieving banking costs similar to international levels," he said.

A part of the study found that "the most important place for a decrease in costs of credit is the reduction of banking administration costs, whose weight contributes to around 5.5 percent of annual lending rates." Average lending rates are 28.3 percent in pesos and 13.4 percent in dollars.
But these challenges are likely to be surmountable, economists said.
Stark of Invesco said there are reasons to be confident "Argentina will in fact stay the course. We see a very favorable environment for long-term investors."
And, the recent decision by Standard & Poor's to raise several Argentine corporations and banks above the sovereign rating ceiling to BBB-, was greeted by most as a very positive signal.
"It would be difficult to give an investment grade rating if S&P did not expect continuity in macro-economic stability and current economic policy," undersecretary Kiguel said.
((--Buenos Aires Newsroom, 541 318-0668 e-mail: axel.bugge@reuters.com))
